Abstract
Agent skills are modular bundles of instructions, code, and resources that an agent
loads on demand, increasingly authored and validated on frontier models and
shared as an open standard. The same skill behaves differently across models: a
strong model turns it into a large performance gain, while a weak model realizes
little of that gain and sometimes does worse than with no skill at all. Cost and
resource constraints, however, often restrict real deployments to exactly these
weaker agents. We hypothesize that the strong model silently supplies procedural
steps the skill leaves implicit, which the weak model omits, and formalize closing
this gap asSkill Transfer: holding the skill’s capability ceiling and the model’s
parameters fixed, we adapt the skill so a specific weak agent can execute it well.
Our method abstracts strong and weak trajectories into typed execution structures,
localizes their structural divergence with a graph edit distance (GED), and repairs
the skill through an iterative diagnoser-patcher loop. Across three benchmarks
and two model families, Skill Transfer raises pass rate over the unmodified skill
significantly and well over other skill-evolution baselines. The adapted skill also
improves the strong agent it was never adapted for, and transfers out of distribution
to a structurally related, unseen task. Code is available at https://github.com/
Yifan-Lan/Skill-Transfer.
1 Introduction
Large Language Model agents solve complex tasks by interleaving reasoning [32, 31, 39, 15] with
actions over an external environment [38, 26, 37], demonstrating excellent performance. However,
they often lack knowledge of some specific domains where fine-tuning is expensive and harmful to
general capability. To solve this, agent skills have been proposed, serving as reusable file systems
where procedural domain knowledge is structurally packaged [ 2]. Specifically, an agent skill is a
self-contained bundle of natural-language instructions, runnable scripts, and reference material that
the agent loads only when a task matches. Skills are compositional, interpretable, and portable.
An agent can accumulate a library of them and reuse it on unseen tasks [ 28, 34, 19], and recent
open standards let a skill authored once be shared across different agents and providers [3, 21]. By
design, skills are expected to work effectively across various agents, agnostic to specific harnesses
and models.
However, Li et al. [16] report that the same curated skills yield various levels of gains across models
and harnesses, demonstrating that some agents improve substantially while others gain little. In
addition, Yu et al. [40] show that skills of different granularity suit different agents, and a skill that
benefits one agent can even harm another. Furthermore, we find a sharper form of this mismatch.
Given one fixed skill, a strong and a weak agent not only differ in task success rate but alsofollow
markedly different procedures, a divergence we quantify with graph edit distance (GED) over their
execution trajectories [25, 9]. Figure 1 illustrates this mismatch. The skill itself is effective for the
strong agent. The weak agent leaves much of its value unrealized because it omits procedural steps
that the strong agent supplies implicitly. This raises a natural question:

Can the full value of the skill be recovered for the weak agent without retraining it?
We formalize the problem of closing this gap asSkill Transfer. Specifically, given a skill that is already
effective for a strong agent, we modify it so that a specific weak agent can use it effectively. We
realize Skill Transfer by abstracting the strong and weak agents’ trajectories into a shared structural
representation, localizing their procedural gaps, and iteratively patching the skill to close them.
This problem matters for deployment. Real-world systems increasingly rely on smaller, cheaper
agents to meet cost, latency, and resource constraints [45, 35], whereas the strongest models remain
expensive and resource-intensive. Skill Transfer lets such deployments reuse the large and growing
corpus of skills authored for frontier models, rather than discarding them or retraining the model.
Our contributions are as follows:
• We formalizeSkill Transfer, the problem of adapting a skill that already works well for a
strong agent so that a weak agent can use it effectively.
• We propose a trajectory-comparison method that abstracts strong and weak trajectories
into typed execution structures, localizes their structural gaps, and repairs the skill with a
diagnoser–patcher agent pair.
• We show across multiple benchmarks and agents that Skill Transfer substantially closes the
strong–weak gap without modifying the weak agent.
2 Related Work
Memory Learning.A line of work improves an agent without weight updates by accumulating
experience in an external memory: storing and retrieving observations, reflections, or long-term
records [23, 22, 46, 36, 7], and distilling past trajectories into reusable, transferable insights [43, 27,
5, 29]. Such memory is auxiliary experience gathered at test time; in contrast, a skill is an authored,
self-contained procedure that an agent loads on demand, and our work transfers this skill to a target
agent rather than growing an experience store.
Skill Evolution.Several works grow or optimize a skill library so that an agent solves more tasks:
accumulating executable skills through self-practice [28, 44], discovering and refining them from
execution feedback [1, 42, 19, 30], or evolving them via reinforcement learning [34]. These methods
raise a skill’s absolute capability to solve more tasks, and do not distinguish the agent a skill was
written for from the agent that has to run it. We instead adapt an existing skill effective on the strong
agent to a weak agent, taking the gap between strong and weak trajectories as the signal. MASA [ 40]
also claims that a skill should be adapted to different backbones, but conditions skill evolution on a
pre-specified model card, a coarse profile that is largely unavailable for closed-source models.
Agent Distillation.Distillation is a complementary route to transfer capability into a smaller
model’s parameters—from classical output [11, 12] to fine-tuning smaller LLMs on teacher-generated

3 Method
Skill Transfer proceeds in four steps. It first abstracts weak and strong trajectories into typed execution
structures (§3.2), then localizes where the weak procedure structurally diverges from the strong one
on each task (§3.3), then synthesizes the systemic gaps across the whole training batch (§3.4), and
finally repairs the skill by turning each diagnosed gap into a targeted edit (§3.5). §3.6 states which
agent carries out each step and how the steps iterate until the skill converges. Figure 2 gives an
overview.
3.1 Problem Formulation

configurations and, at inference time, the same skill; they differ only in their backbone model. A task

3.4 Multi-Case Gap Synthesis
§3.3 types the gaps on a single task. However, a skill edit that chases one task will not generalize,
so this step applies that typing to every task in the training batch T and synthesizes the results.
Besides the paired structures {X (t)s },{X (t)w } and the current skill, it reads a per-task validator report,
a finer-grained comparison of πw’s output against πs’s than R (Appendix C), as well as earlier
iterations’ gap reports and patch history.
Per-task gaps describing the same weakness are grouped across tasks into a set of systemic gaps
G={g 1, g2, . . .}. Each g∈G carries a gap type, metadata (label, description), and two case sets:
Fg ⊆ T, the tasks where πw failed with the gap present, and Pg ⊆ T, the tasks where πw passed
despite it. A gap is admitted for repair if |Fg| ≥1or |Pg| ≥2. The second condition catches a gap
that has not yet caused a failure but recurs in runs that passed anyway, which we treat as a latent
robustness risk rather than a non-issue.

3.5 One-Shot Skill Patching
Given the ranked gap report of §3.4, this step applies the edits it describes in a single consolidated
pass:
• Read and group: read every admitted gap’s patch hint and group hints by the target file section
they name.
•Synthesize: for each affected section, design one coherent edit satisfying every hint touching it.
•Apply: replace the old text that needs editing in all sections in one multi-section edit.
• Verify: re-read the patched skill, confirm every gap in the repair queue has been fixed and no
section contradicts another.

4 Experiments
4.1 Setup
Data.We evaluate on three benchmarks, each with 20 and 30 further cases for training and
validation. SpreadsheetBench [17] collects real-world spreadsheet-manipulation requests from online
forums; each task gives the agent an input workbook and an instruction (e.g. insert a formula, reformat
a range, filter rows); we use a 200-case test split. OfficeQA [8] poses grounded numerical-reasoning
questions over historical U.S. Treasury Bulletin documents, requiring the agent to locate the relevant
table across long, noisy source text and compute a numeric answer; we use a 70-case test split.
DABench [13] poses data-analysis questions over tabular CSV files, requiring the agent to write and
execute analysis code and report a closed-form answer; we use a 150-case test split.

4.3 Structural Convergence
ˆ︁GED decreases monotonically from no skill through original skill and EvoSkill to Skill Transfer in
4 of 8 configurations (both gpt-based weak agents on SpreadsheetBench and OfficeQA), and Skill
Transfer reaches the lowest ˆ︁GED in 7 of 8. Where the pattern holds, it shows that Skill Transfer
closes the procedural gap identified in §3.3 rather than improving outputs incidentally. The weak
agent has learned some of the procedural steps the strong agent performs.
4.4 Skill Transfer Also Benefits the Strong Agent
Although Skill Transfer targets the weak agent’s procedural gap, Table 6 shows the adapted skill also
raises the strong agent’s own pass rate on SpreadsheetBench, from 67.5% to 76.5–81.3% depending
on which weak agent the skill was adapted for. A patch that makes an implicit step explicit does not
only help a weak model that would skip the step totally; it also helps a stronger model that performs
the step inconsistently. The adapted skill converts latent or inconsistent capability into more reliable
behavior, benefiting the strong agent too.
4.5 Out-of-Distribution Generalization
We test whether a skill adapted on one benchmark transfers to a structurally related but distinct task:
WikiTableQuestions [24] (WTQ), where the agent answers a natural-language question about a table
by writing the result into a spreadsheet cell rather than editing a workbook. Table 7 reports results for
both weak agents, using the xlsx skill adapted on SpreadsheetBench. For gpt-4.1-mini, accuracy
on 250 held-out WTQ questions rises from 44.4% to 69.2% (+24.8pp). For gpt-5.4-mini, accuracy
rises from 75.6% to 77.6% (+2.0pp) – a much smaller gain, consistent withgpt-5.4-mini’s already-
high accuracy under the original skill leaving less headroom to close. The skill was never trained
on WTQ; the gains come from the same xlsx-handling procedure (e.g. correct cell addressing,
formula evaluation, output placement) that Skill Transfer made explicit for SpreadsheetBench. The
generalization demonstrates that Skill Transfer does not overfit on specific tasks, but truly closes the
procedural gaps between weak and strong agents.
5 Conclusion
We formalizedskill transfer: given a skill already effective for a strong agent, transfer it to a specific
weak agent without touching that agent’s parameters. Our method abstracts both agents’ trajectories
into typed execution structures, localizes their gaps with a graded graph edit distance, and repairs
the skill through an iterative diagnoser–patcher loop. Across three benchmarks and four weak
agents from two model families, Skill Transfer raises pass rate over both the unmodified original
skill and a skill-evolution baseline, and ˆ︁GED decreases toward the strong agent’s structure in most
configurations, so the gain comes from closing the procedural gap of §3.3. The adapted skill also
improves the strong agent it was never adapted for, and transfers to a related task it was never trained
on. However, two conditions bound the method. First, it needs a strong agent and a small set of tasks
that the agent solves, since the strong trajectories are the reference the diagnoser diffs against; without
such a reference there is no gap to localize. Second, the gain depends on why the weak agent fails.
Procedural failures are largely recoverable by making the missing steps explicit, whereas failures
bound by capability the weak model does not have are difficult to recover from. Within these bounds,
skill transfer offers a training-free route to reusing the growing corpus of skills authored for frontier
models on the smaller, cheaper agents that real deployments often require.
